rubric.text: A closure is a function together with access to its surrounding lexical environment.

examples: Password + MFA creates an authenticated session for user 42.

rubric.text: The process of verifying who a user or service is.
Before granting access, the system needs a trustworthy identity.

examples: user role can read reports; admin role can delete accounts.

rubric.text: The process of deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to do.
Identity alone is not permission.
authorization still happens per action/resource.

examples: createCounter() returns a function that keeps access to count after createCounter returns.

rubric.text: A function plus access to the lexical variables from the scope where it was created.
Closures power encapsulation, callbacks, hooks, and private state patterns.

supporting: A closure lets a function retain access to its lexical environment after the outer function has finished.

examples: Authorization: Bearer <jwt> containing sub, exp, and roles.

rubric.text: A compact signed token format containing claims, represented as header.payload.signature.
It lets a recipient verify that claims were issued by a trusted signer without a database lookup for every verification.

supporting: JWTs are signed claim containers, not automatically encrypted.

examples: SLO 99.9% successful requests over 30 days -> 0.1% error budget.

rubric.text: An SLO defines a reliability target;
the error budget is the allowed unreliability within that target.

supporting: SLOs turn reliability into an explicit product target;
error budgets help decide when to prioritize stability over feature velocity.

rubric.text: An explicit model of allowed states and transitions.
It prevents impossible UI combinations in complex flows.

passages.pageText: SHELF SAMPLES / 03 A closure keeps access A closure is a function together with access to its surrounding lexical environment. The function can keep accessing that environment after the outer call has returned. function counter() { let value = 0; return () => { value += 1; return value; }; } const next = counter(); next(); // 1 next(); // 2 Two separate calls to counter() create two independent environments. SHELF / ORIGINAL SAMPLE NOTES 3

passages.pageText: SHELF SAMPLES / 01 Design Patterns Make the boundary visible A pattern is useful when it makes a recurring design problem easier to understand. It is not a requirement to put every application behind layers of indirection. Contract Adapter System For a PDF reader, a small interface for storing library metadata lets the application service work with a disk implementation or a test double. A new engineer should know what a module owns before reading its implementation. SHELF / ORIGINAL SAMPLE NOTES 1

passages.pageText: SHELF SAMPLES / 01 JavaScript Deep Dive Know the return shape Choosing an array method starts with the shape you need back. One item, a new array and a yes-or-no answer are different results. items.find(test); // item or undefined items.filter(test); // array items.some(test); // boolean items.every(test); // boolean Find selects the first matching value. Filter creates an array containing matching values. Some asks whether a match exists; every asks whether all visited items pass. A boolean cannot be followed by .map(). Check the return value before chaining methods. SHELF / ORIGINAL SAMPLE NOTES 1

rubric.text: Choosing an array method starts with the shape you need back.

passages.pageText: SHELF SAMPLES / 03 Keys describe identity A stable key helps React match an item to its previous instance within a list of siblings. Reordering should not make one item inherit the local state of another. items.map(item => ( <Row key={item.id} item={item} /> )); An array index can be a poor key when items move, are inserted or removed. A freshly generated random key also destroys continuity between renders. Practice: explain why editing a row can reveal a bad key choice. SHELF / ORIGINAL SAMPLE NOTES 3
